data.claim: Optional event fields fold to defaults; new kind is reported by skipped-kinds
data.falsifier: an old event fails to fold or sets a non-empty new field
data.question: Do old events and an old ddflow survive new optional bug fields and a new event kind?

chunk_findings.detail: The handler fabricates a send timestamp for reports that were never sent. Every other field merge (`upstream_url`, `upstream_number`, `upstream_delivery`, `upstream_digest`) leaves the field empty when the event carries nothing, but `upstream_sent_at` falls back to `ev.ts`. The docstring itself calls out the "prepared report with no url yet" case, i.e. an event that records a *proposal*, not a delivery: folding `bug.reported_upstream {delivery: "proposed", digest: "..."}` at t1 sets `bug.upstream_sent_at = t1`, so a report that was only prepared is recorded as sent. Worse, because the merge never replaces, a later real report event `{url: "https://…", delivery: "sent"}` that omits `sent_at` (the schema marks `sent_at` optional) cannot correct it — `str(d.get("sent_at","") or "")` is `""`, then `or bug.upstream_sent_at` keeps t1, so the bug ends up claiming it was sent at the proposal time t1 rather than when it actually went out. Any status/readout keyed on `upstream_sent_at` (the field name promises "sent", and the intent distinguishes "mode propose" from an actual report) will report a proposed report as already delivered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py:_h_bug_reported_upstream (`bug.upstream_sent_at = ... or ev.ts`)

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP `bug_found` tool's declared payload was widened from `("id",)` to `("id", "offer")`, but the upstream offer is, by the stated design, produced only when the call's scope is `ddflow` ("When scope is ddflow the result ends with a one-line offer"). Scope defaults to `project` in this very hunk — `scope=a.get("scope", "") or "project"` — so the common case is a call with no scope argument. Given input `ddflow_bug_found(summary="x")` (no `scope`), the underlying `bug_found` result has no offer, yet the payload spec unconditionally advertises `"offer"` as a returned key. If the payload extractor indexes the listed keys directly (the contract a fixed payload tuple normally encodes), the default project-scope path raises `KeyError`, i.e. the tool fails for every existing caller that never passed a scope; if it uses `.get`, the response shape for all pre-existing project-scope clients changes to include a spurious/`None` `offer` field, which contradicts "the result ends with a one-line offer" only for ddflow. Either way the payload should be conditional on scope, or the api must be guaranteed to always emit an `offer` key (empty for project); as written the unconditional `"offer"` in the tuple is inconsistent with the conditional production of the offer.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py (bug_found `"payload": ("id", "offer")`)

chunk_findings.detail: `upstream_offer(scope, bid)` is called with the *requested* `scope`, never with the scope stored on the bug, and `bid = id or auto_id("B", summary, item)` does not encode `scope`. Concretely: file `bug_found(repo, summary="crash on load", item="T1", scope="ddflow")` and then call `bug_found(repo, summary="crash on load", item="T1")` (the CLI/MCP call for a plain re-report, where `scope` defaults to `"project"`). The second call reuses the same `bid`, and because the append always emits `"scope": scope` (unlike `title`/`severity`, which are dropped when empty via `extra`), it writes a `bug.found` event carrying `scope="project"` for a bug that was filed as ddflow, and `upstream_offer("project", bid)` returns `""`, so the result that should end with the upstream-report offer for that ddflow bug has no `offer` at all. The symmetric case is equally wrong: an existing `scope="project"` bug re-filed with `scope="ddflow"` (same summary+item → same id) returns `offer="This bug is in ddflow itself: …"` even though the record is the project's own bug. The function names the bug's scope in its docstring but has no access to the record's scope, so any call whose requested scope differs from the stored scope produces an offer that is either missing or false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py:upstream_offer / bug_found

chunk_findings.detail: The handler unconditionally stamps a delivery timestamp on reports that were never delivered. The event shape is `{url, number, delivery, sent_at, digest}`, and a *real* delivery always carries `sent_at`; consequently the fallback `or ev.ts` can only ever fire for events that omit it — i.e. the "prepared" / `mode propose` reports the intent describes (offer to prepare a report, `delivery="propose"`, no url yet). For such an input `{"delivery": "propose"}` (no `sent_at`), the line evaluates to `"" or bug.upstream_sent_at or ev.ts` and stores `upstream_sent_at = ev.ts`, so a merely-proposed report is recorded as if it had been sent. Any consumer that treats a non-empty `upstream_sent_at` as proof of delivery (and the field exists precisely to distinguish "prepared" from "went upstream") will mis-report a proposal as delivered, and if the report is never actually filed the bogus timestamp is never corrected. The safe behaviour is to leave `upstream_sent_at` empty for a `delivery`/`sent_at`-less event, since the merge already preserves an earlier real value.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/model.py `_h_bug_reported_upstream` (the `upstream_sent_at` assignment)

chunk_findings.detail: The upstream offer is computed only after the extension branch returns, so a ddflow-scoped report that merges into an existing open bug never gets it. Input: an open bug whose auto id matches (`auto_id("B", summary, item)` is unchanged), plus an `answer` that makes `DD.check_add` return `chk.extension` truthy, with `scope="ddflow"`. The function takes `if chk.extension: return DD.extend(log, cfg, chk, "bug.found")` (added above the `offer = upstream_offer(scope, bid)` line), so the returned outcome has no `offer` field, contradicting the stated behavior that "when scope is ddflow the result ends with a one-line offer". The same path also loses the new scope/severity data: only `title` was added to the `DD.Record` passed to `check_add` (`DD.Record(..., title=title, body=summary, item=item)`), while `scope`/`severity` exist only in the literal dict appended inside the later `with log.transaction():` block. `DD.extend` therefore records the title from the record but silently drops the `scope`/`severity`, so a bug the user explicitly scoped to `ddflow` is folded in as an ordinary project bug with no offer to prepare an upstream report.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py `bug_found` — `if chk.extension: return DD.extend(...)`

chunk_findings.detail:
The handler merges every other field with the "empty never blanks a set value" rule, but for `upstream_sent_at` it adds an unconditional fallback to the event timestamp:

```python
bug.upstream_sent_at = str(d.get("sent_at", "") or "") or bug.upstream_sent_at or ev.ts
```

The handler's own docstring says this event also records a report that "was prepared" (not sent) upstream, and `sent_at` is listed as an *optional* event field. So a prepared-only report is recorded as if it had been sent. Concrete input: append `{"kind": "bug.reported_upstream", "subject": "bug-1", "ts": "2025-01-02T03:04:05Z", "data": {"delivery": "proposed", "digest": "..."}}` (no `sent_at`); the resulting `Bug.upstream_sent_at` is `"2025-01-02T03:04:05Z"` even though nothing was sent at that time. Any consumer that treats a non-empty `upstream_sent_at` as "this bug has already been reported/sent upstream" (e.g. to suppress the one-line `offer` on a later `bug found --scope ddflow`, or to render the report as delivered) is then wrong. Because the merge keeps the value once written, a subsequent prepare/propose event cannot clear it either, so the bogus send time is sticky. Setting `upstream_sent_at` only from an explicit `sent_at` (or only when `delivery` indicates an actual send) would avoid marking a merely prepared report as sent.

chunk_findings.detail: This test folds two `bug.reported_upstream` events for subject `B1` without first emitting a `bug.found` event, then asserts that `fold([prepared, sent]).bugs["B1"]` exists and contains the merged upstream fields. A `bug.reported_upstream` event is supposed to annotate an already-existing bug, as the immediately preceding test demonstrates by supplying `bug.found` first. If the handler is update-only (and `fold` is strict), the lookup raises `KeyError` and the test fails. If the handler auto-creates a bug, the test enshrines a phantom bug produced by a stray upstream event (e.g. a malformed log containing only `bug.reported_upstream` for `B1` would materialize a `B1` bug with no summary). Either way the test does not exercise the intended “prepared then sent” sequence on a real bug; it needs a `bug.found` event before the two upstream events.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_bug_scope.py:test_a_later_upstream_event_fills_what_a_prepared_one_left_empty

chunk_findings.detail:
The change drops the `v != "project"` guard so that any truthy `bg.scope` is now copied into the dedupe row. That guard was not dead code: the *old* write path in `api/knowledge.py` emitted `"scope": scope` unconditionally, and the scope parameter defaults to `"project"` (that is exactly why the new code filters `project` out of `extra`). So every bug record created by the previous version has `bug.found` data with `scope == "project"`, and `_h_bug_found` folds it to `bug.scope == "project"`.

Concretely: for an existing store, `st.bugs[c.id].scope == "project"`, so the new comprehension on line 213 produces `{"severity": ..., "scope": "project", ...}` instead of the previous `{"severity": ...}`. A bug created by the new code (scope suppressed at write time, so `bug.scope == ""`) produces a row with no `scope` key at all. Two records that mean the same thing ("project-scoped bug") now yield two different row shapes, and any consumer that inferred "ddflow-scoped bug" from the mere presence of the `scope` key — the invariant the deleted comment spelled out ("`scope` only when it is the unusual one") — will misclassify every legacy project bug, e.g. emitting an upstream-report offer/note for a bug that lives in the project. This is inconsistent with the same change set, which deliberately stops writing `scope` for `project` on the write path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/_dedupe.py:213 (`_dedupe.py` row.update block)

chunk_findings.detail: The change rewrites the default-scope assertion from `("", "", "project")` to `("", "", "")`, so a call such as `ddflow bug found --summary "plain one"` now persists `bug.scope == ""`. The change notes say the accepted domain is `project|ddflow` and that the default is `project`, so `""` is not one of the accepted scope values; the file's own comment (`# an unrecorded scope is project`) is a rationalization that paper-overs the discrepancy rather than fixing it. This matters because the canonical scope string used throughout the feature is `"project"` — the sibling test asserts `K.upstream_offer("project", "B1") == ""`, and the event fixtures use `subject="B1"` with project semantics — so any consumer that branches on `bug.scope == "project"` (or that validates `scope in {"project","ddflow"}`) will no longer classify a normally-reported bug as project. The test change therefore locks in a regression in the persisted scope value instead of catching it: the previous assertion was the only place verifying the stored default, and it now blesses an out-of-domain value.
